title: AP Precalculus — Recap Set A (Unit 1 to 2.10)
question: Recap Set A: 13 questions in topic order from Unit 1 (rates of change, polynomials, rational functions, transformations, models) to 2.10 (sequences, exponential models, residuals, composition, inverses, logarithms); 9 calculations, 4 ideas.
intro:
**13 questions, Unit 1 to 2.10, in topic order.**

- 9 questions ask for a calculation: work it out on paper, then pick A–D.
- 4 questions ask for the idea behind a topic.
- The title of each question names the topic (1.2, 2.5, …).

**A calculator is allowed. Show your working before choosing A–D.**

questions.title: 1.2 · Average rate of change
questions.prompt: \(f(x) = x^2 - 3x\). Find the average rate of change of \(f\) on \([1,\,4]\).
questions.solution_title: Change in output over change in input

questions.title: 1.3 · Rate of change from a table
questions.prompt:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\
\hline
f(x) & 2 & 5 & 10 & 17
\end{array}
\]

Which statement about \(f\) on this interval is true?
choices: The rate of change is constant, so \(f\) is linear
The rate of change is decreasing, so the graph is concave down
The rate of change is increasing, so the graph is concave up
The rate of change is negative, so \(f\) is decreasing
questions.solution:
Differences between consecutive outputs:

\[
\begin{aligned}
5 - 2 &= 3 \\
10 - 5 &= 5 \\
17 - 10 &= 7
\end{aligned}
\]

- The differences grow: the rate of change is **increasing**.
- Increasing rate of change = **concave up**.
- Not linear: a linear function has the same difference every step.
- Not negative: every difference is positive, \(f\) is increasing.

questions.title: 1.5 · Zeros of a polynomial
questions.prompt:
Find all real zeros of

\[
p(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 - 5x
\]
questions.solution_title: Take out the common factor, then factor the quadratic
questions.solution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p(x) &= x\,(x^2 - 4x - 5) \\
&= x\,(x - 5)(x + 1)
\end{aligned}
\]

Each factor gives a zero:

\[
\boxed{x = 0,\quad x = 5,\quad x = -1}
\]

- Not \(5, -1\) only: the factor \(x\) gives the zero \(x = 0\) too.
- Not \(-5, 1\): \((x-5)(x+1)\), so the signs are \(+5\) and \(-1\).

questions.title: 1.9 · Vertical asymptote or hole
questions.prompt:
\[
r(x) = \frac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 - x - 6}
\]

Where is the **vertical asymptote** of \(r\)?
questions.solution_title: Factor first; a common factor is a hole, not an asymptote
questions.solution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
r(x) &= \frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x - 3)(x + 2)} \\
&= \frac{x + 3}{x + 2}, \quad x \ne 3
\end{aligned}
\]

- \(x = 3\) cancels: a **hole** at \(x = 3\).
- \(x = -2\) stays in the bottom: \(\boxed{\text{vertical asymptote } x = -2}\).
- Not \(x = -3\): that makes the top zero, so it is a zero of \(r\), not an asymptote.

questions.title: 1.12 · Transformations
questions.prompt:
The point \((1,\,4)\) is on the graph of \(f\). Let

\[
g(x) = 2\,f(x - 3) + 1
\]

Which point is on the graph of \(g\)?
questions.solution_title: Inside moves x, outside moves y
questions.solution:
- \(x - 3\) inside: shift **right** by \(3\): \(x = 1 \to 4\).
- \(2(\dots) + 1\) outside: stretch by \(2\), then up \(1\): \(y = 4 \to 2\cdot4 + 1 = 9\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
g(4) &= 2\,f(4 - 3) + 1 \\
&= 2\,f(1) + 1 \\
&= 2\cdot4 + 1 \\
&= \boxed{9}
\end{aligned}
\]

- Not \((-2, 9)\): \(x - 3\) shifts right, not left.
- Not \((4, 7)\): the \(+1\) comes after the \(\times2\).

questions.title: 1.13 · Choose the model
questions.prompt:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3\\
\hline
y & 8 & 12 & 18 & 27
\end{array}
\]

The \(x\) values go up by the same amount. Which type of function fits the data?
questions.solution_title: Equal steps in x, constant ratio in y
questions.solution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
12 \div 8 &= 1.5 \\
18 \div 12 &= 1.5 \\
27 \div 18 &= 1.5
\end{aligned}
\]

- Each step **multiplies** \(y\) by the same factor \(1.5\): \(\boxed{\text{exponential}}\).
- Linear would add the same amount each step (\(4, 6, 9\) are not equal).
- Quadratic would have equal second differences (\(2, 3\) are not equal).

questions.title: 2.1 · Arithmetic sequence
questions.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has \(a_1 = 7\) and common difference \(d = 4\). Find \(a_{15}\).

questions.title: 2.2 · Geometric sequence
2.5 · Exponential model in context
questions.prompt: A colony of \(2000\) bacteria **doubles every 6 hours**. About how many bacteria are there after \(15\) hours? (Calculator allowed.)
questions.solution_title: Count the doublings as a fraction
questions.solution:
Number of doublings in \(15\) hours: \(15 \div 6 = 2.5\).

\[
\begin{aligned}
P &= 2000 \cdot 2^{15/6} \\
&= 2000 \cdot 2^{2.5} \\
&\approx 2000 \cdot 5.657 \\
&\approx \boxed{11{,}300}
\end{aligned}
\]

- Not \(8{,}000\): that is \(2\) doublings (12 hours), stopping early.
- Not \(16{,}000\): that is \(3\) doublings (18 hours).
- Not \(10{,}000\): \(2.5\) doublings is **not** \(2.5 \times 2000\); the growth is multiplicative.

questions.title: 2.6 · Residuals
questions.prompt:
A model predicts \(13\) for \(x = 4\); the actual data value there is \(10\). The residual at \(x = 4\) is \(-3\).

What does this residual tell you?
choices: The model **overestimates** the data at \(x = 4\) by \(3\)
The model underestimates the data at \(x = 4\) by \(3\)
The model must be replaced by an exponential model
questions.solution:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{residual} &= \text{actual} - \text{predicted} \\
&= 10 - 13 \\
&= -3
\end{aligned}
\]

- A **negative** residual means the prediction was too high: the model \(\boxed{\text{overestimates}}\).
- One residual says nothing about which model type to use; that needs the whole residual plot.

questions.title: 2.7 · Composition
2.9 · Logarithmic expressions
questions.solution_title: A fraction below 1 needs a negative exponent

questions.title: 2.10 · The logarithmic function
questions.prompt: \(f(x) = \log_b x\) with \(b > 1\). Which statement is true for **every** such base \(b\)?
choices: The domain of \(f\) is all real numbers

takeaway: Unit 1 is about how functions change; Unit 2 is about functions that add (linear) or multiply (exponential), and running them backwards (logarithms).
